overview: This report summarises Assignment 2, which continues the Assignment 1 BBC Urdu pipeline (250 articles; 15,018 sentences and 434,404 tokens after the A1 normalisation, tokenization, lemmatization and stemming). Everything is implemented from scratch in PyTorch/NumPy (no pretrained models, Gensim, HuggingFace or PyTorch Transformer classes); all numbers come from the executed notebook (stored in outputs/results.json) and every component is unit-tested (32 pytest tests). Re-running the unmodified A1 module on raw.txt reproduces cleaned.txt exactly, so each stemmed token can be traced back to its surface form, which Part 2 relies on. Articles were assigned to the five categories of the brief by keyword-guided scoring (Urdu translations of the given keywords, normalised by the A1 pipeline, plus BBC topic tags) with 9 headline-checked corrections: Health & Society 117, International 66, Politics 25, Economy 22, Sports 20. The shared vocabulary is the 10,000 most frequent tokens (99.78% token coverage) plus <UNK>.
part1_a: TF-IDF (10,001 terms × 250 articles, raw-count TF, natural-log IDF) separates the categories well; the most discriminative words are Trump, journalism, media, Modi, journalist, president (Politics), cricket, sport, team, Test, match, runs, player, wicket, captain (Sports), oil, price, petrol, rupees, litre, barrel, diesel, crude, port (Economy), Iran, American, Saudi, missile, agreement, Russia, army (International) and child, police, women, accused, rape, film, doctor (Health & Society). PPMI (window k = 5, 807k positive cells, 0.81% dense) yields sensible neighbours, e.g. court → court (Eng.), case, petition, accused, supreme; oil → crude, barrel, export, strait, Hormuz; the t-SNE of the 200 most frequent content words shows clear clusters of time expressions, money/quantities, cricket vocabulary and country names. The skip-gram model (separate V/U matrices, f3/4 noise table, K = 10, k = 5, d = 100, Adam 0.001, batch 512) was trained for 15 epochs (loss 3.26 → 2.77); the number of epochs, and the decision not to use word2vec sub-sampling, were selected on 180 development analogies disjoint from the reported tests. Its neighbours are topical (court → judge, petition, case, appeal, lawyer; army → commander, military, armed forces) and 5 of the 10 pre-registered analogies are solved within the top 3 (4 at rank 1: Pakistani:Indian, Imran Khan:Shehbaz Sharif, Donald Trump:Narendra Modi, oil:barrel :: petrol:litre; Putin at rank 2), while thinly attested relations (capitals, kinship) fail.
part1_b: PPMI is the strongest representation on the 20 related-word pairs, ahead of skip-gram on the cleaned corpus. Skip-gram on raw text suffers from vocabulary fragmentation (19,423 raw types vs 10,943 cleaned; neighbours are split over izafat-marked and inflected variants), and doubling the dimension (C4) lowers the training loss but not the similarity quality. On a 0.43 M-token corpus, counts are hard to beat and preprocessing matters more than capacity; with 20 pairs, one rank change moves the MRR by up to 0.05.
part2_a: 500 sentences (100 per category, 5–50 tokens) were annotated automatically. The POS tagger uses 12 tags (the 11 listed in the brief plus AUX, since the brief announces 12) and is built on the A1 lemmatizer and stemmer: look-up of the surface form, of its A1 lemma and of its A1 stem in a hand-crafted lexicon (823 nouns, 252 verb lemmas expanded to 3,998 forms, 399 adjectives, 253 adverbs, plus closed classes), A1-suffix morphology, and context rules for ambiguous function words. NER uses a seed gazetteer of 86 Pakistani persons, 121 locations and 71 organisations (+44 foreign persons, 56 MISC entries) with longest-match look-up and a given-name pattern, producing BIO tags. The split is 350/75/75 sentences, stratified by topic; the test set has 2,036 tokens and 55 entities. The 2-layer BiLSTM (128 units per direction, dropout 0.5 between the layers, C3 initialisation, padding excluded from the loss) uses a from-scratch CRF with Viterbi decoding for NER, Adam (10<super>-3</super>, weight decay 10<super>-4</super>) and early stopping on validation F1 (patience 5).
part2_b: Fine-tuning the embeddings is clearly better than freezing them (mean validation F1 89.2 vs 82.2 for POS and 70.4 vs 48.0 for NER), so the fine-tuned models are reported and saved. The POS model reaches 89.8% token accuracy and 87.8 macro-F1 on the test set (seed 42); its most confused pairs are NOUN–UNK (UNK is assigned by the rule-based tagger to otherwise unknown words), NOUN–ADJ (the A1 stemmer removes the adjectival suffix -i) and NOUN–VERB (conjunct verbs). The NER BiLSTM-CRF obtains P/R/F1 = 68.0/61.8/64.8 with conlleval (LOC 78.6, MISC 63.2, PER 52.6, ORG 18.2); most errors are entities whose tokens never occur in the 350 training sentences (e.g. Peshawar, Anwar Ibrahim, Geo News), names merged by the stemmer (Saud = Saudi) and incomplete silver labels. Backward context is essential (unidirectional: −5.4 POS, −23.5 NER), the pretrained embeddings help (random initialisation: −4.2 POS, −11.4 NER), the CRF adds 7.5 NER points over a softmax layer, and dropout makes no significant difference once early stopping is used.
part3_a: Each article is represented by its first 256 cleaned tokens (249 of 250 articles are truncated); the stratified split has 175/38/37 articles. The encoder follows the brief exactly — scaled dot-product attention with a padding mask, 4 heads with separate 128→32 projections and a shared output projection, a 512-unit FFN, a fixed sinusoidal positional-encoding buffer, 4 Pre-LN blocks, a learned [CLS] vector and a 128→64→5 MLP (2.08 M parameters) — and was trained with AdamW (5×10-4, weight decay 0.01) and a cosine schedule with 50 warm-up steps for 20 epochs. It stays at the majority-class accuracy (47.4%) for 7 epochs and reaches 68.4% validation accuracy at epoch 11; the best-validation checkpoint gives 78.4% test accuracy and 72.9 macro-F1 (Sports 3/3, Health & Society F1 0.91, Politics F1 0.29 on only 3 articles). In the final layer, [CLS] attention concentrates on topic words, e.g. the three occurrences of cricket in a Sports article receive about 7× more attention than any other token.
part3_b: The Transformer is more accurate than a BiLSTM classifier trained on the same split (+6.3 accuracy and +10.5 macro-F1 points on average), while the BiLSTM converges in fewer epochs and is 2.4× faster per epoch: self-attention is quadratic in the 257 positions and our multi-head layer runs four separately projected heads, whereas the LSTM is one optimised kernel with fewer parameters. For 200–300 articles we recommend the Transformer for this task because topic labels depend on which keywords occur, which attention pooling captures directly; but with 37 test articles its advantage amounts to only 2–3 articles and its macro-F1 varies by ±7 points across seeds, so the cheaper BiLSTM remains a reasonable alternative.
conclusion: All components required by the brief were implemented from scratch and evaluated on the BBC Urdu corpus from Assignment 1. Three lessons stand out: with 0.43 M tokens, careful preprocessing and simple count statistics matter more than model capacity (PPMI ≥ skip-gram, d = 200 ≤ d = 100); bidirectional context, pretrained embeddings and CRF decoding each add 4–24 F1 points in sequence labelling even with 350 training sentences; and attention pooling over a [CLS] token was the better topic classifier for 175 training articles. During development a shared-memory bug (nn.Embedding.from_pretrained on torch.as_tensor shares the NumPy array, so fine-tuned models silently modified the common embedding matrix) was found by re-loading the saved models, fixed, covered by a regression test, and all results were regenerated. The main limitations are the silver-standard (rule-based) POS/NER labels and the small test sets (55 entities, 37 articles), which make differences of a few points uncertain — hence the three-seed reporting. Code, data splits, models and the executed notebook are in the repository.
